lead: Analog pulse modulation sends a pulse every T<sub>s</sub> seconds and lets one pulse property follow the sample: height in PAM, width in PWM, position in PPM. The pulse rate stays fixed at the sampling rate. PAM is the first step towards PCM and TDM; PWM drives motors, lamps and class-D amplifiers; PPM appears in optical and infrared links. This chapter shows how each is made, what bandwidth it needs, and why constant-height pulses resist amplitude noise.
prereq: You need: sampling and the aperture effect and the spectrum of a rectangular pulse.

sections.h3: PAM: pulse height follows the sample

blocks.text: Take a pulse train with period Ts = 1/fs, pulse width τ and duty cycle d = τ/Ts, with fs ≥ 2fm. In pulse amplitude modulation (PAM) pulse n has height m(nTs), or A + m(nTs) when an offset A keeps every pulse positive. Natural PAM lets the top follow m(t) during the pulse; flat-top PAM holds the sample for τ, so a sample-and-hold makes it.
Flat-top PAM is the sampled message filtered by one rectangular pulse, so its spectrum is
P(f) = fs τ sinc(fτ) Σ M(f − kfs)

Each copy of M(f), at 0, ±f<sub>s</sub>, …, is shaped by τ sinc(fτ), which has its first null at 1/τ. Natural PAM instead gives undistorted copies weighted by d sinc(kd), so only flat-top PAM has the aperture effect.
The receiver lowpass filters at fm; for flat-top PAM it adds a 1/sinc equalizer if τ is not small. PAM is still analog: it becomes digital only after quantization and coding in PCM.

sections.h3: PWM and PPM: timing carries the sample

blocks.text: Pulse width modulation (PWM), also called pulse duration modulation (PDM), keeps the height fixed and sets the width τn = τ0 + kw m(nTs), where τ0 is the unmodulated width and kw the width sensitivity in s/V. A comparator against a sawtooth of period Ts makes it: the output is high until the sawtooth crosses the message, so one edge (here the leading edge) stays fixed and the trailing edge moves. A lowpass filter recovers m(t), because the average of a PWM wave is proportional to its duty cycle.

Pulse position modulation (PPM) keeps height and width fixed and shifts the whole pulse from its nominal position by kp m(nTs). It is made from PWM: differentiate the PWM wave, keep only the trailing-edge spikes, and let each trigger a monostable that gives one short pulse of fixed width. That is one pulse per sampling period, placed where the PWM pulse ended. The receiver needs a timing reference, usually from a sync pulse, to measure each shift.

The bandwidth of a pulse train is set by its fastest feature. PAM pulses of width τ need roughly 1/(2τ) to 1/τ. PWM and PPM carry the message in edge timing, so the edges must be sharp: a rise time t<sub>r</sub> needs about 1/(2t<sub>r</sub>) of bandwidth, and t<sub>r</sub> must be far shorter than the smallest width or shift to be resolved. PPM, with the narrowest pulses, needs the most.

With constant height, a receiver can slice the pulses at half height and ignore most amplitude noise; noise then matters only through the timing jitter it causes on a sloping edge. PWM wastes power because wide pulses carry energy without extra information, which PPM avoids. Since every PAM pulse uses only τ of each Ts, other channels can fill the gaps: that is time division multiplexing.

examples.question: A 1 kHz tone is sampled at 8 kHz and sent as flat-top PAM with 25 µs pulses. Find T<sub>s</sub>, the duty cycle, the first spectral null and the aperture loss at 1 kHz and at 3.4 kHz.
steps: First null of τ sinc(fτ): f = 1/τ = 1/(25 × 10⁻⁶ s) = 40 × 10³ Hz = 40 kHz.
Loss at 1 kHz: sinc(1000 × 25 × 10⁻⁶) = sinc(0.025) = 0.9990, that is −0.009 dB.
Loss at 3.4 kHz: sinc(0.085) = 0.9882, that is −0.10 dB. Compare the 2.75 dB of a full-width hold (τ = T<sub>s</sub>) in the sampling chapter.
examples.answer: T<sub>s</sub> = 125 µs, d = 20 %, first null 40 kHz; with τ only a fifth of T<sub>s</sub> the aperture loss is under 0.1 dB, so no equalizer is needed.

examples.question: PWM uses f<sub>s</sub> = 10 kHz, τ<sub>0</sub> = 50 µs and k<sub>w</sub> = 10 µs/V, with the leading edge at the start of each slot. Four samples are +2, +1, −1 and −3 V. Find each width, each trailing-edge time, and the shift of each PPM pulse made from those edges.
steps: T<sub>s</sub> = 1/10 kHz = 100 µs, so the slots start at 0, 100, 200 and 300 µs.
Unmodulated edges would be at 50, 150, 250 and 350 µs, so the PPM shifts are +20, +10, −10 and −30 µs (k<sub>p</sub> = k<sub>w</sub> = 10 µs/V).
Check the range: every width stays inside 0 to 100 µs, so no pulse merges with the next; the limit is |m| < 5 V.
examples.answer: Widths 70, 60, 40, 20 µs; trailing edges at 70, 160, 240, 320 µs; PPM shifts +20, +10, −10, −30 µs, one pulse per 100 µs period.

traps: PAM is not PCM: PAM is analog until it is quantized and coded.
PPM shifts a fixed-width pulse; PWM changes the width. PPM from PWM uses one edge per period, not both edges, which would double the pulse rate.
Duty cycle is τ/T<sub>s</sub> (dimensionless), not τ·T<sub>s</sub>.
The first null of a rectangular pulse of width τ is at 1/τ, not 1/(2τ).

quiz.q: Which pulse parameter carries the message in PAM, PWM and PPM?
quiz.a: PAM: amplitude. PWM: width (duration). PPM: position in time.

quiz.q: Why does flat-top PAM need an equalizer when τ is close to T<sub>s</sub>?
quiz.a: The hold shapes the spectrum by τ sinc(fτ). When τ is near T<sub>s</sub> the sinc falls noticeably inside the message band (2.75 dB at 3.4 kHz for 8 kHz sampling), so a 1/sinc equalizer restores the top of the band.

quiz.q: A 2 kHz tone is sampled at 10 kHz with 20 µs flat-top pulses. Find T<sub>s</sub>, the duty cycle and the first null.
PWM has τ<sub>0</sub> = 40 µs and k<sub>w</sub> = 8 µs/V at f<sub>s</sub> = 12.5 kHz. Find the width for m = −2.5 V and the largest |m| allowed.
quiz.a: τ = 40 + 8(−2.5) = 20 µs. T<sub>s</sub> = 80 µs, so 0 < 40 + 8m < 80 gives |m| < 5 V.

quiz.q: Why are PWM and PPM less sensitive to amplitude noise than PAM?
quiz.a: Their height is constant, so the receiver slices at half height and reads only edge times. Noise affects them only through the jitter it adds on a sloping edge, which sharp edges keep small. PAM puts the message in the height, so the same noise adds straight to the sample.

quiz.q: Order PAM, PWM and PPM by bandwidth and explain.
quiz.a: PAM < PWM < PPM. PAM needs only enough bandwidth to keep its τ-wide pulses separate. PWM and PPM carry the message in edge timing, so they need fast edges; PPM also has the narrowest pulses, so it needs the most.

beyond: Not for the exam. PWM is the language of power electronics: class-D amplifiers, motor drives and LED dimmers switch rather than amplify. Four-level PAM (PAM4) carries two bits per symbol in fast serial and optical links. Search next for class-D amplifiers and PAM4 signalling.
